nameStory: Smooth Beggarticks gets its name from two key features: the 'smooth' refers to its hairless leaves and stems, while 'beggarticks' comes from the plant's sneaky seed-dispersal strategy. The seeds have sharp barbs that grab onto fur, clothing, and anything else that brushes by, clinging like persistent beggars who won't let go until they've hitched a ride to a new home.
description: Smooth Beggarticks is a tall, wetland-loving member of the sunflower family that can grow anywhere from knee-high to well over your head—sometimes reaching 6 feet tall! It produces cheerful yellow daisy-like flowers with about 7-8 bright petals surrounding a golden center. The plant has narrow, lance-shaped leaves with finely toothed edges, and after flowering, the heavy seed heads characteristically droop downward. This annual or short-lived perennial thrives in wet places and is known for its clingy, barbed seeds that hitchhike on passersby.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow daisy-like blooms with 7-8 ray petals (each up to an inch long) surrounding a golden center of tiny disc flowers. The flowers have a fresh, slightly sweet scent and feel papery to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves 2-6 inches long with finely serrated edges that feel slightly rough along the margins. The leaves are smooth and hairless (hence 'smooth' beggarticks) with a somewhat glossy surface.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Dark, wedge-shaped seeds topped with 2-4 sharp, backward-pointing barbs that feel prickly and grab onto clothing or fur with surprising tenacity. Seeds develop after flowers fade and are contained in drooping seed heads.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, upright plant that can tower over 3 feet, often growing in dense colonies along water edges. Stems are smooth and often reddish-tinged, branching near the top where flower clusters form.

idTips.label: Fruit Behavior
idTips.description: After flowering, the heavy seed heads bend downward in a characteristic nodding position, making the plant look like it's bowing. This drooping behavior becomes more pronounced as seeds ripen.

habitat: Look for Smooth Beggarticks in consistently moist to wet areas throughout New England, especially along pond edges, stream banks, marshes, and coastal estuaries. It thrives in muddy or sandy soils that stay wet most of the year and often grows alongside cattails, sedges, and other water-loving plants. You'll commonly spot it in disturbed wetlands, drainage ditches, and the muddy edges of seasonal ponds.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge in late spring as small rosettes of narrow leaves. Early growth is often hard to distinguish from other wetland plants until the characteristic leaf shape becomes clear.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from mid to late summer when the bright yellow flowers are most abundant and conspicuous. This is the best time for identification as the distinctive daisy-like blooms make the plant unmistakable.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed heads develop their characteristic drooping posture. The barbed seeds ripen and become incredibly clingy—you'll know you've brushed against this plant when seeds stick to your clothes.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems may persist with dried, drooping seed heads still attached. The plant dies back to the roots (if perennial) or dies completely (if annual), leaving little trace above ground.

funFact: Smooth Beggarticks seeds are so effective at hitching rides that they inspired the invention of Velcro—the Swiss engineer who created it was actually studying how burdock burrs (a related plant) stuck to his dog's fur, leading to the hook-and-loop fastener that revolutionized how we stick things together!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with Nodding Beggarticks, which has very similar drooping seed heads and yellow flowers. The key difference is in the leaves: Smooth Beggarticks has simple, undivided leaves, while Nodding Beggarticks often has leaves divided into 3-5 leaflets. Memory trick: 'Smooth and Simple' go together—smooth beggarticks has smooth, simple leaves.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being native to the Americas, Smooth Beggarticks is considered uncommon in New England with only 36 recorded observations, making it a special find for nature explorers. The name 'beggarticks' is sometimes spelled as one word or hyphenated as 'beggar-ticks,' and the plant is also called 'bur-marigold,' though it's not related to true marigolds—it just shares their sunny yellow color.
compareHints: Among its many Bidens relatives in New England, Smooth Beggarticks stands out for its simple, undivided leaves (unlike Three-parted Beggarticks) and its prominent yellow ray petals (unlike Devil's Beggarticks which often lacks showy petals entirely). It's most similar to Nodding Beggarticks but lacks that species' tendency toward divided leaves, making the leaf shape the most reliable way to distinguish between these two wetland cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's many beggarticks species, Devil's Beggarticks is distinguished by its three-part leaves (versus simple leaves in Nodding Beggarticks) and its lack of showy petals (unlike the bright yellow rays of Tickseed Sunflower).

Among New England's many beggarticks species, Nodding Beggarticks is the easiest to identify because of its drooping flowers - Devil's Beggarticks has upward-facing flowers and deeply divided leaves, while Smooth Beggarticks has much larger, showier flowers that face outward.
Among New England's many beggarticks species, Purplestem stands out for its smooth stems with purple coloring and relatively few flower heads per plant.
Unlike its weedy beggarticks relatives that grow in damp soil and are known for their sticky seeds, Water Marigold is the aquatic specialist of the family.
Among New England's beggarticks, Tall Beggarticks stands out for its height and hairy stems.

Unlike its freshwater cousins like Devil's Beggarticks or Nodding Beggarticks, Estuary Beggarticks has evolved to handle salt stress, giving it thicker, more succulent leaves and limiting it to coastal habitats.

Among its many beggarticks relatives, swamp beggarticks stands out for its complete lack of ray petals (the showy outer petals), unlike nodding beggarticks or smooth beggarticks which have yellow rays.

Among New England beggarticks, Three-parted is unique for its deeply three-divided leaves - Devil's Beggarticks has simple oval leaves, while Spanish Needles has finely divided, almost fern-like foliage.
Among New England's many beggarticks species, Tickseed Sunflower stands out for having showy yellow petals - many of its relatives like Devil's Beggarticks have tiny or no petals at all.

Among its beggarticks relatives, Spanish needles stands out with its finely divided, feathery leaves - most other Bidens species have simple oval leaves or leaves divided into just 3-5 broad segments.
Among New England's beggarticks, Bearded Beggarticks stands out for its large, showy yellow petals - most other species like Devil's Beggarticks have tiny or no petals at all.

Marsh Tickseed stands out from its beggarticks relatives by being strictly a wetland specialist - while cousins like Devil's Beggarticks grow in disturbed soils and gardens, Marsh Tickseed demands consistently soggy conditions.
Among its many beggarticks relatives, Eaton's is unique for its salt marsh habitat - most others prefer freshwater wetlands or disturbed soils.
White beggarticks stands out from its many beggarticks relatives because of its prominent white petals - most other species in the genus have small, inconspicuous flowers or yellow petals.
